findings.suggestion: Batch the durable writes: one transaction per pass with a multi-row update (or a JDBC batch of `update links set click_count = click_count + ? where id = ?`) instead of one transaction per link, and pipeline the settle decrements. Then raise flush-batch-size and measure drain rate against arrival rate. To confirm before shipping: expose `HLEN clicks:pending` as a gauge and alert if it trends upward — a monotonically growing pending hash is the signal that the drain is behind, and it is currently invisible.
findings.summary: The click drain has a hard throughput ceiling of 500 distinct links per 5s pass (app.click.flush-batch-size=500, flush-interval=PT5S), and each link costs one JPA transaction plus one Redis settle round trip, executed sequentially on a single scheduler thread. That is ~100 links/second per instance. Above that arrival rate of *distinct* clicked links, the Redis pending hash grows without bound: nothing ever removes fields faster than they are added, and the backlog is what feeds PERF-2. The service's stated scale (A2 reasons about 100M links/day) is three to four orders of magnitude above this ceiling. Every instance runs the same unsharded schedule, so adding replicas multiplies the read of the same hash rather than dividing the work.

findings.suggestion: Replace HGETALL with a cursor: `HSCAN key cursor COUNT n` in a loop inside the script until `limit` fields are collected, persisting the cursor (or using a per-pass random start) so passes make progress across the hash. The zero-field sweep can stay on the scanned window. To confirm: `redis-cli --latency` and the `latency history command` event, or SLOWLOG, during a pass with a synthetically large pending hash.
findings.summary: readPending bounds what it *returns* (limit) but not what it *reads*: the script calls HGETALL on the entire pending hash and then discards everything past the limit. The batch is therefore not bounded at all in cost — it is O(total pending links) in Redis CPU and in Lua-side memory, every 5 seconds, on every instance. Redis executes scripts single-threaded, so a pass over a hash that has grown to hundreds of thousands of fields (see PERF-1) blocks the same Redis instance that serves the resolution cache and the rate limiter on the redirect hot path. The failure couples: a click-counting backlog becomes redirect latency, and the 1s command timeout then converts it into cache misses and fail-open rate limiting rather than an outage — but it is the hot path degrading because of a background job.

findings.suggestion: Fetch all pending deltas for the page in one call: `opsForHash().multiGet(pendingKey, codes)` (HMGET is single-key, so it keeps the Cluster-safety property the class documents), and do it after the transaction returns rather than inside it. The same fix applies to reading the delta once per page instead of once per row.
findings.summary: GET /api/v1/links maps every row through toResponse, which calls clickCounter.pendingDelta per link — one Redis HGET per item, sequential, up to 100 per request (MAX_PAGE_SIZE). This is a textbook N+1 against the cache tier, and it happens inside a readOnly @Transactional that has already acquired a Hibernate connection for the page query, so a Hikari connection is pinned for the whole串 of Redis round trips. With the configured 1s Redis timeout, a degraded-but-alive Redis makes one list request occupy a database connection for up to 100 seconds; ten such requests exhaust the default pool of 10 and stall every other endpoint, including a redirect that missed cache.

findings.suggestion: Drop @Transactional from resolve() and let the repository call use its own transaction, then perform cache.put after it returns. Confirm with a connection-hold histogram (Hikari `hikaricp.connections.usage` is already exported via the Prometheus registry) comparing hit and miss requests.
findings.summary: resolve() is @Transactional(readOnly = true) and the cache write (cache.put, a Redis round trip) happens inside that transaction, after the JDBC statement has acquired a connection. Hibernate's delayed acquisition means a cache *hit* costs no connection — good — but every *miss* holds a pooled connection across a Redis PUT with a 1s timeout. Under a miss storm (see PERF-5) that is connection-hold time proportional to Redis latency rather than to database latency, on the one path that must not queue. The transaction also buys nothing here: it wraps a single read.

findings.suggestion: Set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size explicitly with a comment tying it to expected concurrency and PostgreSQL max_connections, and consider per-code single-flight (a striped lock or Caffeine-style loading wrapper around the miss path) so a hot link's TTL expiry produces one database read rather than one per in-flight click. Measure: hikaricp.connections.pending and the redirect miss ratio under a sustained load test.
findings.summary: No connection pool sizing is configured, so Hikari runs at its default maximum of 10 connections, and nothing configures the Lettuce or Tomcat side either. That interacts with a structural property of the design: app.cache.ttl is pinned at 60s to floor the takedown bound, so every actively-clicked link must be re-read from PostgreSQL at least once per minute per replica, and there is no single-flight — N concurrent clicks arriving on a link whose entry has just expired all miss and all issue the same lookup. The redirect's database read rate therefore has a floor of (distinct active links)/60s, served through 10 connections. It is an indexed unique lookup on ux_links_domain_code so each is cheap, but the pool, not the query, is the ceiling, and nobody has picked the number deliberately.

findings.suggestion: Reject anything failing `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$` at the top of follow() with the same notFound() response (identical body and headers, so it stays indistinguishable), before touching the cache or the database. This costs nothing and removes both the Redis key-space and the database round trip for malformed codes.
findings.summary: The redirect accepts any path segment as a code with no length or charset bound before spending work on it. AliasPolicy caps codes at 64 characters and the column is VARCHAR(64), yet a multi-kilobyte path still becomes a Redis GET key, a PostgreSQL query parameter, and — on a miss — a negatively-cached Redis entry keyed by the full garbage string. Cost per request is small and 60s TTLs bound the memory, but it is work and cache space an attacker chooses the size of, on the one endpoint that is unauthenticated and rate-limited only per-IP.

findings.suggestion: If the totals must stay in the contract, at least bound `page` (or cap offset) the way `size` is capped in requireValidPaging. Longer term, keyset pagination on (created_at desc, code asc) removes both the count and the offset walk. Confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the count query against a customer with ~1M links.
findings.summary: findOwnedBy returns Page, so Spring Data issues a `select count(...)` alongside every list request, and LinkPage exposes totalElements/totalPages so it cannot be dropped without an API change. The count scans the whole customer_id range of ix_links_owner_listing on every page request — for a customer with a large link inventory that is the expensive half of the request, repeated for each page. Offset paging compounds it: `page` is unbounded, so page=100000 makes PostgreSQL walk and discard the offset rows. This is a management endpoint, not the hot path, so the blast radius is one caller's latency and the connection they hold.

findings.suggestion: Bound password hashing with a semaphore (or a small dedicated executor) sized to available cores, returning 503/429 when saturated, so credential-stuffing load cannot displace the redirect path. Measure: heap allocation rate and p99 redirect latency while replaying concurrent sign-in failures.
findings.summary: Every sign-in attempt — including every failed one, deliberately, for timing-equality — runs Argon2id at m=16384 KiB, t=2. Nothing bounds how many run concurrently: Tomcat's default 200 request threads means up to 200 simultaneous hashes, ~3.2 GiB of transient heap allocation and full CPU saturation, from unauthenticated requests. The sign-in bucket (60/min/IP) is the only brake and it fails open when Redis is unreachable, which is precisely when the service is already unhappy. Cost of being wrong is a GC-thrashing JVM that also stops serving redirects, since they share the same thread pool and heap.

findings.suggestion: Two cheap options that keep the exactness guarantee: pipeline the rate-limit and cache-GET into one round trip (both are needed unconditionally), and/or issue the HINCRBY asynchronously on the Lettuce connection without awaiting the reply, so the 302 is not gated on it — this differs from the executor-with-a-queue the javadoc rightly rejects, since it drops nothing. At minimum, lower the Redis command timeout for the increment specifically, and measure the redirect p99 with a latency-injected Redis (`CLIENT PAUSE` or a toxiproxy) to see the tail the current arrangement produces.
findings.summary: The analytics write is on the critical path, and this is a documented deliberate trade (ClickCounter's javadoc, AC3) rather than an oversight — but the shape is worth stating plainly: a served redirect makes three *sequential* Redis round trips (rate-limit script, cache GET, click HINCRBY) before the 302 is written, four on a not-found. Each carries the 1s command timeout, so a Redis that is slow rather than down can add up to ~3s to a redirect that would otherwise be served entirely from cached data. The increment in particular delays the response purely to record a statistic.

findings.suggestion: Either store and query email lower-cased (as threat_denylist.host already does, with the comment explaining exactly this reasoning), or add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_email_lower ON customers (lower(email))` and query with a matching predicate. Confirm with EXPLAIN on the generated statement.
findings.summary: findByEmailIgnoreCase generates `upper(email) = upper(?)`, which cannot use the ux_customers_email btree index in V1__initial_schema.sql — every sign-in is a sequential scan of customers. Today that is two seeded rows and there is no registration endpoint, so the cost is nil; it is filed only because the index exists and reads as if it serves this lookup, and the day accounts arrive the scan arrives with them.

not_examined: Actual query plans — no database was available to me, so index usability is inferred from the migration DDL and the derived-query naming, not from EXPLAIN output.
JVM heap sizing, GC behaviour and allocation rates; the Argon2 memory arithmetic in PERF-8 is from the encoder's documented parameters, not measured.
Ed25519 JWT verification cost per management request (JwtVerifier/jjwt+BouncyCastle) — it is off the redirect path and I did not benchmark it.

Lettuce connection multiplexing behaviour under saturation: I assumed the shared non-pooled connection the Redis starter configures by default and did not verify how it queues commands when Redis is slow.

Tomcat thread pool, request body size caps and max-http-request-header sizes — all left at Spring Boot defaults, none configured in application.yml, and I did not trace what those defaults are in Boot 3.5.16.

Redis deployment topology, memory limits and eviction policy (docker-compose.yml read only for pool/limit settings) — whether the cache tier is allowed to evict under pressure decides what PERF-2's growing hash actually does.
The test suite's own runtime and Testcontainers behaviour; the build is reported green and I did not run it.

Behaviour of the flush job with more than one replica beyond what RedisClickCounter's javadoc asserts — I took the non-destructive read/settle invariant on trust rather than reasoning through every interleaving.
Anything requiring a profiler: allocation hot spots, serialization cost of Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer per cache read on the redirect path, and actual per-request CPU.
summary: The core hot path is well built: the redirect is a single indexed (domain, code) lookup behind a Redis cache that also caches misses, clicks never touch PostgreSQL synchronously, the rate limiter is one atomic single-key Lua call that fails open, and both the unique constraint and the concurrent-alias race are handled correctly. At the load this service will plausibly see on day one, the redirect is fine. The problems are all in the machinery around it, and two are structural rather than micro. First, the click drain cannot keep up by construction: 500 links per 5s pass, one transaction and one Redis round trip each, means ~100 distinct links/second per instance against a design that reasons about 100M links/day — the pending hash only grows. Second, the drain reads that hash with HGETALL and discards everything past the limit, so the batch bounds output but not cost; a backlog therefore turns into a single-threaded Redis stall every 5 seconds, on the same Redis the redirect depends on. Those two compound each other and are the findings worth acting on. Third and independent: the list endpoint does one Redis HGET per row inside a transaction holding a database connection, which is an N+1 that pins a pool connection for up to 100 sequential Redis timeouts. The remainder are smaller — an unsized connection pool under a cache TTL that is pinned at 60s by the takedown bound (so database read rate has a floor and there is no single-flight on a miss), an unbounded code length reaching the cache and database, count-plus-offset paging, unbounded concurrent Argon2 hashing, and a non-indexable email lookup that costs nothing today. I could not measure any of this; the severities reflect mechanisms I can read in the code, and I have said where I am extrapolating to load nobody has run.
